title: heavy vehicle braking
objectives: Explain why heavy vehicles take longer to stop than smaller passenger vehicles
Describe the basic scientific principles of braking, including how friction converts motion into heat
Identify the elements that make up total stopping distance
State the effects of doubling weight and speed on the stopping power required
Explain how to brake safely on ice, downgrades, water and with ABS-equipped combination vehicles

sections.title: Power to move, power to stop and stopping distance
points: An engine converts heat energy into motion; brakes do the opposite, converting motion back into heat through friction.
Brake linings rub against drums, or pads against rotors; the heat is absorbed and dissipated mostly through the drums/rotors.
A loaded tractor-trailer may take over one kilometre and one minute to reach 100 km/h, but must stop far faster.
An emergency stop in about seven seconds needs roughly nine times the acceleration force — about 4,000 hp of stopping force.
With 16 brakes sharing the work, a few out-of-adjustment brakes overload the rest and lengthen stopping distance.
Total stopping distance is see-think-do: perception, reaction, brake lag and braking time combined.
Heavy vehicle drivers should never follow closer than five seconds at highway speeds.
mustKnow: An average driver's reaction time is about 3/4 of a second (plus about 3/4 of a second perception time)
Air brake lag time is approximately 4/10 of a second between applying and the brakes beginning to function
Total stopping time = perception time + reaction time + brake lag time + braking time
Heavy vehicles: never less than five seconds behind the vehicle ahead at highway speeds
Stopping a tractor-trailer in seven seconds takes about nine times the acceleration force — approximately 4,000 hp

check.q: What is the approximate brake lag time of an air brake system?
check.explanation: Air brakes have a lag of about 4/10 of a second between application and the brakes functioning.

check.q: At highway speeds, how far behind the vehicle ahead should a heavy vehicle driver stay?
check.explanation: Drivers of buses, trucks and other large heavy vehicles should never be less than five seconds behind.

sections.title: Speed, weight and brake heat
points: More speed or more weight means more stopping power is needed and a longer stopping distance.
Doubling speed quadruples the stopping power needed; doubling weight doubles it; doubling both needs eight times.
Trucks and buses have bigger brakes and more linings than cars, yet still take longer to stop.
Going downhill lengthens stopping distance because of gravity; going uphill shortens it.
Excessive hard braking builds heat faster than brakes can dissipate it; hot drums expand away from the linings.
Too much heat causes brake fade, brake damage or failure — components or tires can even catch fire.
mustKnow: 2 x vehicle speed requires 4 x the stopping power
2 x vehicle weight requires 2 x the stopping power
2 x speed and 2 x weight together require 8 x the stopping power
Brakes heat to about 120 degrees C in normal stopping and should not exceed about 250 degrees C under hard braking
Heavy tractor-trailer combinations can weigh up to 63,500 kg when loaded

check.q: If you double your vehicle's speed, how much more stopping power do you need?
check.explanation: Doubling speed requires four times the stopping power; doubling weight only doubles it.

check.q: What temperature should brake components not exceed under hard braking?
check.explanation: Brakes operate best around 120 degrees C and should not exceed about 250 degrees C.

sections.title: Retarders
points: Retarders provide auxiliary slowing, such as controlling speed on long downgrades, saving the main brakes for emergencies.
The four main types are engine, exhaust, hydraulic driveline and electric driveline retarders.
Many retarders can absorb as much or more horsepower than the engine develops.
Engine retarders work best at higher engine r.p.m. and lower vehicle speed, so select your gear before the hill.
On slippery roads, retarders can lock the drive wheels, stall the engine, or even jackknife a tractor-trailer.
Obey municipal signs restricting engine retarder/engine brake use.
mustKnow: Four main types of retarders: engine, exhaust, hydraulic driveline, electric driveline
Engine retarders are most effective at higher r.p.m. with the transmission in a low gear
Select your gear before you start down a hill — you're more likely to miss a shift on the downgrade

check.q: When is an engine retarder most efficient?
choices: At low r.p.m. and high speed
At higher r.p.m. and lower vehicle speed
Only when the brakes are hot
check.explanation: Engine retarders are more efficient at a higher engine r.p.m. and a lower vehicle speed.

check.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four main types of retarders?
check.explanation: The four main types are engine, exhaust, hydraulic driveline and electric driveline retarders.

sections.title: Braking technique: ice, downgrades, water and runaway lanes
points: On ice, use extremely light brake pressure — a slowly revolving wheel grips better than a locked, skidding wheel.
Use snow tires and/or properly sized, tightly mounted chains; mount them in chain-up areas, not on the hill.
Descend in a lower gear than you climbed with; never shift to a higher gear on a downgrade unless speed is controlled.
Pick a safe speed, a low gear and the retarder so you can descend without using the service brakes.
If speed still climbs, brake hard enough to drop 10 to 15 km/h, then downshift, and repeat as needed.
Through water, keep a slight drag on the brakes, then apply light pressure afterward to dry them out.
Runaway lanes beside downhill grades are only for slowing or stopping when brakes fail — never for anything else.
mustKnow: Fines up to $2,000 for operating a vehicle with brakes not adjusted correctly or not performing adequately
On a downgrade, apply brakes hard enough to reduce speed by 10 to 15 km/h, then downshift to a lower main gear
Almost all brake failures and downhill runaway crashes are caused by poor speed control (overdriving the brakes)
Keep your vehicle in gear all the way down the hill

check.q: If speed keeps rising on a downgrade, how much should each brake application reduce your speed?
check.explanation: Apply the brakes hard enough to reduce speed by 10 to 15 km/h, then downshift to a lower main gear.

check.q: What should you do with the brakes while driving through water on the roadway?
choices: Place a slight constant drag on them
check.explanation: A slight drag on the brakes reduces the amount of water entering the brake drums and shoes.

sections.title: Combination braking, ABS and traction control
points: In an air brake vehicle, all brakes apply at the same time and the same pressure when you press the pedal.
Braking too hard, or using only trailer brakes on slippery roads, can lock wheels and cause a skid or jackknife.
Brakes, tires and suspension work best when the vehicle is legally loaded and weight is properly distributed among axles.
ABS prevents wheel lockup from overbraking on slippery surfaces, but doesn't let you drive faster or stop sooner.
With ABS, apply firm, continuous pedal pressure — never pump — and expect normal noise, movement and shudder.
If tractor and trailers don't all have ABS, brake as if the combination has no ABS.
ATC uses the ABS wheel sensors to brake a spinning drive wheel and can reduce engine power in slippery conditions.
mustKnow: ABS is mandatory in Canada on all trucks and buses over 4,560 kg manufactured since April 1, 2000, and on all commercial trailers with air brakes
A full jackknife occurs when tractor and trailer form an angle of 90 degrees or less — possible even at very low speeds
On some surfaces such as gravel, braking distance with ABS may be longer

check.q: What is the correct way to make an emergency stop with ABS?
choices: Pump the brakes on and off
Apply firm, hard continuous pressure until the vehicle stops
check.explanation: Pumping turns ABS on and off; apply firm, continuous pressure to the brake pedal until stopped.

check.q: ABS is mandatory on trucks and buses over what weight manufactured since April 1, 2000?
check.explanation: ABS is mandatory on all trucks and buses over 4,560 kg built since April 1, 2000.

summary: Brakes are heat machines: friction converts the energy of motion into heat, which drums and rotors must absorb and dissipate.
Total stopping distance adds perception, reaction, brake lag and braking time — so heavy vehicles keep at least five seconds back.
Doubling speed needs four times the stopping power; doubling weight doubles it; both together need eight times.
Control downgrade speed with a low gear and retarder so service brakes stay cool; overheating causes brake fade and failure.
With ABS, brake firmly and continuously without pumping; know which units in a combination have ABS before you need it.
